title: Der Eisenofen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 127. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 127 turns on a promise made under duress: a princess lost in the forest strikes a bargain with a talking iron stove to get home again, and once she has broken her word — speaking one sentence too many to her own father — she must go find the stove, and the enchanted prince inside it, all over again, across a glass mountain, a stretch of razor swords and a wide water, aided only by gifts from a hut of toads. Three walnuts hide three ever finer gowns, which she trades to a false bride for three nights beside the drugged, unknowing prince, until on the third night he wakes and knows her voice. It belongs to the same family as Cupid and Psyche — a wife who must earn back a husband she nearly lost through one broken condition.

sentences.t: Zur Zeit, wo das Wünschen noch geholfen hat, ward ein Königssohn von einer alten Hexe verwünscht, daß er im Walde in einem großen Eisenofen sitzen sollte.
sentences.l: In the time when wishing still helped, a king’s son was cursed by an old witch, that he should sit in the forest in a great iron stove.
sentences.i: In the days when wishing still helped, a king’s son was put under a spell by an old witch, so that he had to sit in the forest inside a great iron stove.
sentences.n: Zur Zeit, wo das Wünschen noch geholfen hat is one of the tales’ openings, standing beside Es war einmal: the old time when a wish still had power. das Wünschen is the infinitive used as a noun, “the wishing”. ward is the older past of werden and carries the passive here. The Eisenofen is no kitchen stove but a great iron furnace-chest, big enough to shut a man inside — which is the whole plot.

sentences.t: Da brachte er viele Jahre zu, und konnte ihn niemand erlösen.
sentences.l: There he passed many years, and no one could deliver him.
sentences.i: There he spent many years, and no one could set him free.
sentences.n: zubringen — to pass, to spend, of time (separable: brachte … zu). In konnte ihn niemand erlösen the verb stands before its subject because the clause hangs on the opening Da. erlösen, to release or redeem from a spell, is the word this tale turns on and it comes back again and again.

sentences.t: Einmal kam eine Königstochter in den Wald, die hatte sich irre gegangen und konnte ihres Vaters Reich nicht wieder finden: neun Tage war sie so herum gegangen und stand zuletzt vor dem eisernen Kasten.
sentences.l: Once a king’s daughter came into the forest, she had gone herself astray and could not find her father’s kingdom again: nine days had she gone about so and stood at the last before the iron chest.
sentences.i: One day a king’s daughter came into the forest; she had lost her way and could not find her father’s kingdom again. Nine days she had gone about like that, and at last she stood before the iron chest.
sentences.n: sich irre gehen — to go astray, with the reflexive sich; modern German says sich verirren. ihres Vaters Reich puts the genitive first, as English does in “her father’s kingdom”. der Kasten is a chest or box: the stove is named a second way, and the reader is meant to see a great iron box standing in the wood.

sentences.t: Da kam eine Stimme heraus und fragte sie „wo kommst du her, und wo willst du hin?“
sentences.l: Then a voice came out and asked her “where do you come from, and where do you want to go?”
sentences.i: Then a voice came out and asked her, “where do you come from, and where are you going?”
sentences.n: woher and wohin are pulled apart in speech: wo … her, “where from”, and wo … hin, “where to”. willst du hin again leaves the verb of motion out after wollen — German does not need it.

sentences.t: Sie antwortete „ich habe meines Vaters Königreich verloren und kann nicht wieder nach Haus kommen.“
sentences.l: She answered “I have lost my father’s kingdom and cannot come home again.”
sentences.i: She answered, “I have lost my father’s kingdom and cannot find my way home again.”
sentences.n: nach Haus is the fixed direction phrase, “homeward”. The girl has not lost the kingdom in the sense of forfeiting it; she has lost her way to it.

sentences.t: Da sprachs aus dem Eisenofen „ich will dir wieder nach Haus verhelfen und zwar in einer kurzen Zeit, wenn du willst unterschreiben zu thun was ich verlange.
sentences.l: Then it spoke out of the iron stove “I will help you home again, and that in a short time, if you will sign to do what I demand.
sentences.i: Then a voice spoke out of the iron stove, “I will help you home again, and that in a short time, if you will put your name to doing what I ask.
sentences.n: sprachs is sprach es run together — “it spoke”, with no speaker named. verhelfen takes the dative of the person helped, dir. und zwar pins down what was just said: “and that indeed”. unterschreiben is the language of a written bond — what is asked of her is a signature, and it binds. The speech runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t: Ich bin ein größerer Königssohn als du eine Königstochter, und will dich heirathen.“
sentences.l: I am a greater king’s son than you a king’s daughter, and will marry you.”
sentences.i: I am a greater king’s son than you are a king’s daughter, and I mean to marry you.”
sentences.n: als du eine Königstochter leaves the verb out — German does not repeat “are” in such a comparison. heirathen is the 1857 spelling of heiraten.

sentences.t: Da erschrack sie, und dachte „lieber Gott, was soll ich mit dem Eisenofen anfangen!“
sentences.l: Then she took fright, and thought “dear God, what am I to begin with the iron stove!”
sentences.i: Then she took fright and thought, “dear God, what am I to do with an iron stove!”
sentences.n: erschrack, 1857 for erschrak, is the intransitive erschrecken: to be startled, to take fright. etwas mit jemandem anfangen — “to begin something with”, that is, to make anything of. soll asks what is expected of her, not what she owes.

sentences.t: Weil sie aber gerne wieder zu ihrem Vater heim wollte, unterschrieb sie sich doch zu thun was er verlangte.
sentences.l: But because she gladly wanted home again to her father, she signed herself after all to do what he demanded.
sentences.i: But because she longed to be home again with her father, she bound herself in writing after all to do what he asked.
sentences.n: sich unterschreiben — to put one’s name to a thing, to bind oneself in writing; the reflexive sich makes the bond fall on her. wollte again with no verb of motion, carried by heim. doch marks that she does it in spite of her fright.

sentences.t: Er sprach aber „du sollst wiederkommen, ein Messer mitbringen und ein Loch in das Eisen schrappen.“
sentences.l: But he said “you shall come back, bring a knife along and scrape a hole in the iron.”
sentences.i: But he said, “you shall come back, bring a knife with you and scrape a hole in the iron.”
sentences.n: schrappen is a homely word for scraping; the tale sets it beside schaben for the same work and uses both. mitbringen, to bring along, is separable but stands whole in the infinitive.

sentences.t: Dann gab er ihr jemand zum Gefährten, der gieng nebenher und sprach nicht: er brachte sie aber in zwei Stunden nach Haus.
sentences.l: Then he gave her someone as a companion, who went alongside and did not speak: but he brought her home in two hours.
sentences.i: Then he gave her someone for a companion, who walked beside her and did not speak; but he brought her home in two hours.
sentences.n: zum Gefährten — “as a companion”, with zu where English says “for”. Nothing is ever said about who this silent companion is or where he came from; the tale lets him go without a word. gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging.

sentences.t: Nun war große Freude im Schloß, als die Königstochter wieder kam, und der alte König fiel ihr um den Hals und küßte sie.
sentences.l: Now there was great joy in the castle when the king’s daughter came again, and the old king fell about her neck and kissed her.
sentences.i: Now there was great joy in the castle when the king’s daughter came back, and the old king fell on her neck and kissed her.
sentences.n: jemandem um den Hals fallen — to throw one’s arms round someone’s neck; the person embraced stands in the dative, ihr.

sentences.t: Sie war aber sehr betrübt und sprach „lieber Vater, wie mirs gegangen hat!
sentences.l: But she was very grieved and said “dear father, how it has gone with me!
sentences.i: But she was much cast down and said, “dear father, how it has gone with me!
sentences.n: mirs is mir es. wie mirs gegangen hat is the impersonal turn, “how it has gone for me”, that is, what has befallen me. The speech runs on into the next unit, so no closing quotation mark comes yet.

sentences.t: ich wäre nicht wieder nach Haus gekommen aus dem großen wilden Walde, wenn ich nicht wäre bei einen eisernen Ofen gekommen, dem habe ich mich müssen dafür unterschreiben, daß ich wollte wieder zu ihm zurück kehren, ihn erlösen und heirathen.“
sentences.l: I would not have come home again out of the great wild forest, if I had not come upon an iron stove; to it I have had to bind myself in writing in return, that I would come back to it again, deliver it and marry it.”
sentences.i: I would never have come home again out of the great wild forest if I had not come upon an iron stove; and I have had to sign myself over to it in return — that I would come back to it, set it free and marry it.”
sentences.n: bei einen eisernen Ofen gekommen has the accusative einen where the grammar wants the dative einem: spoken usage, printed as it stood in 1857. mich müssen unterschreiben stacks two infinitives after habe, the older order. zurück kehren is zurückkehren, to return, with the particle standing free. She speaks of the stove throughout as dem, ihn — “it” — though it is “it” she has promised to marry.

sentences.t: Da erschrack der alte König so sehr, daß er beinahe in eine Ohnmacht gefallen wäre, denn er hatte nur die einzige Tochter.
sentences.l: Then the old king took fright so much that he would almost have fallen into a faint, for he had only the single daughter.
sentences.i: Then the old king was so frightened that he almost fell into a swoon, for she was his only daughter.
sentences.n: in Ohnmacht fallen — to fall into a faint, to swoon. beinahe … gefallen wäre uses the subjunctive for what nearly happened and did not.

sentences.t: Berathschlagten sich also, sie wollten die Müllerstochter, die schön wäre, an ihre Stelle nehmen; führten die hinaus, gaben ihr ein Messer und sagten sie sollte an dem Eisenofen schaben.
sentences.l: [They] took counsel together then: they would take the miller’s daughter, who was beautiful, in her place; led her out, gave her a knife and said she should scrape at the iron stove.
sentences.i: So they took counsel together: they would put the miller’s daughter, who was beautiful, in her place. They led her out, gave her a knife and told her to scrape at the iron stove.
sentences.n: The subject is simply left out at the head of the sentence — Berathschlagten sich also, with no sie; the bracketed [They] is supplied here so that the English can stand, and marks a word the 1857 text does not have. sich berathschlagen (1857 -th-) is to take counsel together. die schön wäre is the subjunctive of reported speech: beautiful, as they said.

sentences.t: Sie schrappte auch vier und zwanzig Stunden lang, konnte aber nicht das geringste herabbringen.
sentences.l: She scraped too for four and twenty hours long, but could not bring down the least little bit.
sentences.i: She scraped away for a full four and twenty hours, but could not get the least bit off it.
sentences.n: vier und zwanzig stands as two words in 1857 where modern German writes vierundzwanzig. das geringste is the superlative of gering, “the least thing, the least little bit”. herabbringen — to bring down, that is, to get anything off the iron.

sentences.t: Wie nun der Tag anbrach, riefs in dem Eisenofen „mich däucht es ist Tag draußen.“
sentences.l: When now the day broke, it called in the iron stove “me it seems it is day outside.”
sentences.i: Now when day broke, a voice called in the iron stove, “it seems to me it is day outside.”
sentences.n: wie here means “when”, not “how”; you will meet it constantly in the tales. riefs is rief es. mich däucht is an old impersonal turn — “it seems to me”, with the person in the accusative; modern German has mich dünkt, and the verb has all but died out. anbrechen, of the day, is to break.

sentences.t: Da antwortete sie „das däucht mich auch, ich meine ich höre meines Vaters Mühle rappeln.“
sentences.l: Then she answered “that seems so to me too, I think I hear my father’s mill clattering.”
sentences.i: Then she answered, “so it seems to me too; I think I hear my father’s mill clattering.”
sentences.n: ich meine here is “I think, it seems to me”, not “I mean”. rappeln is to rattle or clatter; the sound of the mill in her head gives her away, and the voice in the stove catches it at once.

sentences.t: „So bist du eine Müllerstochter, dann geh gleich hinaus und laß die Königstochter herkommen.“
sentences.l: “So you are a miller’s daughter, then go straight out and let the king’s daughter come here.”
sentences.i: “Then you are a miller’s daughter: go out at once and let the king’s daughter come here.”
sentences.n: laß … herkommen — lassen with a bare infinitive, “let come, have come”. herkommen is to come here, toward the speaker.

sentences.t: Da gieng sie hin und sagte dem alten König der draußen wollte sie nicht, er wollte seine Tochter.
sentences.l: Then she went there and said to the old king the one outside did not want her, he wanted his daughter.
sentences.i: So she went and told the old king that the one out there would not have her: he wanted his daughter.
sentences.n: The daß that would introduce the reported speech is simply left out, as speech leaves it out. der draußen — “the one outside”, with the article standing alone as a pronoun.

sentences.t: Da erschrack der alte König und die Tochter weinte.
sentences.l: Then the old king took fright and the daughter wept.
sentences.n: erschrack again, the third fright in this tale; the daughter’s weeping is set beside it without a word of comment, which is the tales’ way with grief.

sentences.t: Sie hatten aber noch eine Schweinehirtentochter, die war noch schöner als die Müllerstochter, der wollten sie ein Stück Geld geben, damit sie für die Königstochter zum eisernen Ofen gienge.
sentences.l: But they had besides a swineherd’s daughter, she was still more beautiful than the miller’s daughter; to her they would give a piece of money, so that she should go to the iron stove for the king’s daughter.
sentences.i: But they had a swineherd’s daughter as well, who was even more beautiful than the miller’s daughter; they would give her a piece of money to go to the iron stove in the king’s daughter’s stead.
sentences.n: der wollten sie … geben — the demonstrative der is the dative “to her”, put first for emphasis. für die Königstochter here is “in place of”, not “on behalf of”. gienge is the subjunctive, 1857 for ginge, the mood of a purpose not yet carried out.

sentences.t: Also ward sie hinausgebracht und mußte auch vier und zwanzig Stunden lang schrappen; sie brachte aber nichts davon.
sentences.l: So she was brought out and had to scrape for four and twenty hours too; but she brought nothing off it.
sentences.i: So she was taken out and had to scrape for four and twenty hours as well; but she got nothing off it.
sentences.n: ward … hinausgebracht is the passive with the older ward. nichts davon bringen — to get nothing off it: the second girl fails in almost the same words as the first, and the tale means the repetition to be heard.

sentences.t: Wie nun der Tag anbrach, riefs im Ofen „mich däucht es ist Tag draußen.“
sentences.l: When now the day broke, it called in the stove “me it seems it is day outside.”
sentences.i: Now when day broke, the voice called in the stove, “it seems to me it is day outside.”
sentences.n: The same line as before, word for word, with only Eisenofen shortened to Ofen.

sentences.t: Da antwortete sie „das däucht mich auch, ich meine ich höre meines Vaters Hörnchen tüten.“
sentences.l: Then she answered “that seems so to me too, I think I hear my father’s little horn tooting.”
sentences.i: Then she answered, “so it seems to me too; I think I hear my father’s little horn blowing.”
sentences.n: As before, with the mill exchanged for the swineherd’s horn: tüten is to toot, to blow a horn. The swineherd blew his horn through the village at daybreak to call the pigs out.

sentences.t: „So bist du eine Schweinehirtentochter, geh gleich fort und laß die Königstochter kommen:
sentences.l: “So you are a swineherd’s daughter, go away at once and let the king’s daughter come:
sentences.i: “Then you are a swineherd’s daughter: go away at once and let the king’s daughter come —
sentences.n: fortgehen, to go away, with the particle standing alone beside the imperative geh. The colon in 1857 does the work of a dash or semicolon; the speech runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t: und sag ihr es sollt ihr widerfahren was ich ihr versprochen hätte, und wenn sie nicht käme, sollte im ganzen Reich alles zerfallen und einstürzen und kein Stein auf dem andern bleiben.“
sentences.l: and tell her it should befall her what I had promised her, and if she did not come, everything in the whole kingdom should fall apart and cave in and no stone remain upon the other.”
sentences.i: and tell her that what I promised her shall befall her, and that if she does not come, everything in the whole kingdom shall fall apart and cave in, and not one stone stay upon another.”
sentences.n: widerfahren takes the dative — a thing befalls a person, ihr. sollt, hätte, käme, sollte are all subjunctive: the message as it is to be carried and repeated. kein Stein auf dem andern is the old formula of total ruin, taken from the Gospel.

sentences.t: Als die Königstochter das hörte, fieng sie an zu weinen: es war aber nun nicht anders, sie mußte ihr Versprechen halten.
sentences.l: When the king’s daughter heard that, she began to weep: but it was now not otherwise, she had to keep her promise.
sentences.i: When the king’s daughter heard that, she began to weep; but there was no help for it now — she had to keep her promise.
sentences.n: anfangen splits: fieng … an, the 1857 spelling of fing. es war nicht anders — “it was not otherwise”, that is, there was no help for it. ein Versprechen halten, to keep a promise, as in English.

sentences.t: Da nahm sie Abschied von ihrem Vater, steckte ein Messer ein und gieng zu dem Eisenofen in den Wald hinaus.
sentences.l: Then she took leave of her father, put a knife in and went out to the iron stove into the forest.
sentences.i: So she took leave of her father, put a knife in her pocket and went out into the forest to the iron stove.
sentences.n: einstecken — to put in one’s pocket (separable: steckte … ein); what she puts it into is left unsaid. Abschied nehmen von — to take leave of.

sentences.t: Wie sie nun angekommen war, hub sie an zu schrappen und das Eisen gab nach, und wie zwei Stunden vorbei waren, hatte sie schon ein kleines Loch geschabt.
sentences.l: When she had now arrived, she began to scrape and the iron gave way, and when two hours were past, she had already scraped a small hole.
sentences.i: When she had arrived, she set to scraping and the iron gave way, and when two hours were past she had already scraped a small hole.
sentences.n: hub … an is the old past of anheben, “to begin”; modern German says fing an, and hub belongs to the higher, older register. nachgeben — to give way, to yield (separable). The iron yields to her where it would not yield to the others: that is the point, and the tale does not explain it.

sentences.t: Da guckte sie hinein und sah einen so schönen Jüngling, ach, der glimmerte in Gold und Edelsteinen, daß er ihr recht in der Seele gefiel.
sentences.l: Then she peeped in and saw so beautiful a youth, ah, he glimmered in gold and precious stones, that he pleased her right in her soul.
sentences.i: Then she peeped in and saw so handsome a youth — ah, he glittered with gold and jewels — that he pleased her to the very soul.
sentences.n: The sentence breaks off in the middle for the teller’s own ach, and only afterwards comes the daß clause that so … was waiting for; the seam is left standing in the printed text and is kept here. jemandem gefallen takes the dative of the one pleased, ihr.

sentences.t: Nun da schrappte sie noch weiter fort und machte das Loch so groß, daß er heraus konnte.
sentences.l: Now then she scraped still further on and made the hole so big that he could get out.
sentences.i: Now she scraped on further still and made the hole so big that he could come out.
sentences.n: fortschrappen — to scrape on, to keep scraping, with fort, “onward”, thrown to the end. daß er heraus konnte leaves the verb of motion out after konnte.

sentences.t: Da sprach er „du bist mein und ich bin dein, du bist meine Braut und hast mich erlöst.“
sentences.l: Then he said “you are mine and I am yours, you are my bride and have delivered me.”
sentences.i: Then he said, “you are mine and I am yours; you are my bride and you have set me free.”
sentences.n: du bist mein und ich bin dein is an old betrothal formula, known from medieval love verse; mein and dein stand uninflected in it. The words come back at the very end of the tale, and are meant to be recognised there.

sentences.t: Er wollte sie mit sich in sein Reich führen, aber sie bat sich aus daß sie noch einmal dürfte zu ihrem Vater gehen,
sentences.l: He wanted to lead her with him into his kingdom, but she asked out for herself that she might go once more to her father,
sentences.i: He wanted to take her with him into his kingdom, but she begged leave to go to her father once more,
sentences.n: sich etwas ausbitten — to ask a thing for oneself, to beg leave (separable: bat … aus). dürfte is the subjunctive of dürfen, “might be allowed to”.

sentences.t: und der Königssohn erlaubte es ihr, doch sollte sie nicht mehr mit ihrem Vater sprechen als drei Worte, und dann sollte sie wiederkommen.
sentences.l: and the king’s son allowed it to her, only she should speak no more than three words with her father, and then she should come back.
sentences.i: and the king’s son allowed it, only she was to speak no more than three words with her father, and then she was to come back.
sentences.n: nicht mehr … als drei Worte is pulled apart around the verb. sollte here is not duty but the terms laid down: she was to do it so.

sentences.t: Also gieng sie heim, sie sprach aber mehr als drei Worte: da verschwand alsbald der Eisenofen und ward weit weg gerückt über gläserne Berge und schneidende Schwerter;
sentences.l: So she went home, but she spoke more than three words: then at once the iron stove vanished and was shoved far away over glassy mountains and cutting swords;
sentences.i: So she went home, but she spoke more than three words — and at once the iron stove vanished and was carried far away over mountains of glass and cutting swords;
sentences.n: The breaking of the word is told in half a line, with no blame and no reason given; the tales rarely stop to explain. rücken is to shift or shove a thing bodily, so weit weg gerückt is “shoved far away”. Glassy mountains and cutting swords are the standing furniture of the far-off place in these tales — she will have to cross both.

sentences.t: doch der Königssohn war erlöst, und nicht mehr darin eingeschlossen.
sentences.l: yet the king’s son was delivered, and no longer shut in inside it.
sentences.i: yet the king’s son was free, and no longer shut up inside it.
sentences.n: einschließen — to shut in, to enclose; eingeschlossen is its past participle. darin is “in it”, the stove.

sentences.t: Danach nahm sie Abschied von ihrem Vater und nahm etwas Geld mit, aber nicht viel, gieng wieder in den großen Wald und suchte den Eisenofen, allein der war nicht zu finden.
sentences.l: After that she took leave of her father and took some money along, but not much, went again into the great forest and sought the iron stove, only it was not to be found.
sentences.i: After that she took leave of her father and took some money with her, but not much, went into the great forest again and looked for the iron stove; only it was not to be found.
sentences.n: mitnehmen — to take along (separable: nahm … mit). allein at the head of a clause is the older “only, but”, and not “alone”. nicht zu finden sein is the usual German turn for what cannot be found.

sentences.t: Neun Tage suchte sie, da ward ihr Hunger so groß, daß sie sich nicht zu helfen wußte, denn sie hatte nichts mehr zu leben.
sentences.l: Nine days she sought, then her hunger became so great that she did not know how to help herself, for she had nothing more to live on.
sentences.i: Nine days she searched, and her hunger grew so great that she did not know what to do, for she had nothing left to live on.
sentences.n: sich nicht zu helfen wissen — not to know how to help oneself, to be at one’s wits’ end. In nichts mehr zu leben, leben is the verb: nothing left to live on. Nine days again, as at the beginning — the tale counts in nines and threes.

sentences.t: Und als es Abend ward, setzte sie sich auf einen kleinen Baum und gedachte darauf die Nacht hinzubringen, weil sie sich vor den wilden Thieren fürchtete.
sentences.l: And when it became evening, she set herself on a small tree and thought to pass the night on it, because she was afraid of the wild beasts.
sentences.i: And when evening came she settled herself in a small tree, meaning to pass the night up there, because she was afraid of the wild beasts.
sentences.n: gedenken with an infinitive is “to intend, to have in mind”. hinzubringen is hinbringen with the zu pushed inside the verb, as separable verbs take it. sich fürchten vor takes the dative: to be afraid of.

sentences.t: Als nun Mitternacht heran kam, sah sie von fern ein kleines Lichtchen und dachte „ach, da wär ich wohl erlöst,“ stieg vom Baum und gieng dem Lichtchen nach, auf dem Weg aber betete sie.
sentences.l: When now midnight came on, she saw from afar a little light and thought “ah, there I would surely be saved,” climbed down from the tree and went after the little light, but on the way she prayed.
sentences.i: When midnight drew on she saw a little light far off and thought, “ah, there I should surely be saved,” climbed down from the tree and followed the little light; and on the way she prayed.
sentences.n: herankommen — to come on, to draw near (separable). nachgehen takes the dative of what is followed: dem Lichtchen nach. wär is the clipped subjunctive wäre; wohl is “surely, I daresay”. erlöst is the tale’s own word for release from a spell, used here of her own rescue.

sentences.t: Da kam sie zu einem kleinen alten Häuschen, und war viel Gras darum gewachsen, und stand ein kleines Häufchen Holz davor.
sentences.l: Then she came to a small old little house, and much grass had grown about it, and a little heap of wood stood before it.
sentences.i: Then she came to a small old cottage, with much grass grown up around it and a little heap of wood standing before it.
sentences.n: The two clauses that follow begin straight with the verb — und war viel Gras darum gewachsen, “and there had grown much grass about it” — where English needs a “there”. Häuschen and Häufchen are diminutives in -chen, which the tales use constantly.

sentences.t: Dachte sie „ach wo kommst du hier hin!“ guckte durchs Fenster hinein, so sah sie nichts darin, als dicke und kleine Itschen (Kröten), aber einen Tisch, schön gedeckt mit Wein und Braten, und Teller und Becher waren von Silber.
sentences.l: Thought she “ah, where are you coming to here!”, peeped in through the window, and then she saw nothing in it but fat and little Itschen (toads), but a table finely laid with wine and roast meat, and plates and cups were of silver.
sentences.i: She thought, “ah, where have you come to now!”, peeped in through the window, and saw nothing inside but toads, fat ones and little ones — but a table finely laid with wine and roast meat, and the plates and cups were of silver.
sentences.n: The parenthesis (Kröten) is the Grimms’ own, printed in the 1857 text: they use the dialect word Itschen and gloss it for their readers with the standard word for toads. Round brackets in the German are theirs; square brackets in these translations are supplied here. She says du to herself in her dismay, as one does. Braten is the noun, the roast, not the verb braten.

sentences.t: Da nahm sie sich das Herz und klopfte an.
sentences.l: Then she took herself the heart and knocked.
sentences.i: Then she took heart and knocked.
sentences.n: sich das Herz nehmen — to take heart, to summon one’s courage. anklopfen — to knock (separable: klopfte an).

sentences.t: Alsbald rief die Dicke
sentences.l: At once the fat one called
sentences.n: die Dicke is the adjective dick, “fat”, used as a noun: the fat one, the big toad. Adjectives serve as names for these creatures throughout. What she calls is verse, and stands as verse in the printed text.

sentences.t:
„Jungfer grün und klein,
Hutzelbein,
Hutzelbeins Hündchen,
hutzel hin und her,
laß geschwind sehen wer draußen wär.“
sentences.l:
“Maiden green and small,
Shrivel-leg,
Shrivel-leg’s little dog,
shrivel here and there,
let [us] quickly see who was outside.”
sentences.i:
“Maiden green and small,
Shrivel-leg,
Shrivel-leg’s little dog,
hop here and there,
go quickly and see who is outside.”
sentences.n: The German rhymes klein with Hutzelbein and her with wär. Lectorium’s idiomatic line does not rhyme: the sense is given plainly and the rhyme is named here instead. Die Hutzel is a dried, shrivelled pear, so Hutzelbein is something like Shrivel-leg, a name for the little toad; hutzel hin und her turns the name into a verb and is more sound than sense. laß geschwind sehen has no object at all — the bracketed [us] is supplied here so the English can stand, and is not in the 1857 text. wär is the clipped subjunctive wäre, kept for the rhyme.

sentences.t: Da kam eine kleine Itsche herbei gegangen und machte ihr auf.
sentences.l: Then a little toad came walking up and opened for her.
sentences.i: Then a little toad came walking up and opened the door to her.
sentences.n: kommen with a past participle — kam … gegangen, “came walking” — is a common German way of telling how someone arrives. aufmachen, to open (separable: machte … auf); the door itself is left unsaid.

sentences.t: Wie sie eintrat, hießen alle sie willkommen, und sie mußte sich setzen.
sentences.l: As she stepped in, all bade her welcome, and she had to set herself down.
sentences.i: As she stepped in they all bade her welcome, and she had to sit down.
sentences.n: willkommen heißen — to bid welcome. eintreten, to step in (separable: trat ein). mußte sich setzen is the pressing hospitality of hosts, not compulsion.

sentences.t: Sie fragten „wo kommt ihr her? wo wollt ihr hin?“
sentences.l: They asked “where do you come from? where do you want to go?”
sentences.i: They asked, “where do you come from? where are you going?”
sentences.n: The toads address her as ihr, the older respectful “you” for a single person, where the voice in the stove said du. Again wo … her and wo … hin, woher and wohin pulled apart.

sentences.t: Da erzählte sie alles, wie es ihr gegangen wäre, und weil sie das Gebot übertreten hätte, nicht mehr als drei Worte zu sprechen, wäre der Ofen weg sammt dem Königssohn:
sentences.l: Then she told everything, how it had gone for her, and that because she had transgressed the command to speak no more than three words, the stove was gone together with the king’s son:
sentences.i: Then she told them everything, how she had fared, and how, because she had broken the command not to speak more than three words, the stove was gone and the king’s son with it:
sentences.n: wäre, hätte, wäre are all subjunctive — her story as reported by the teller rather than vouched for. das Gebot übertreten — to transgress a command. sammt, 1857 for samt, is “together with” and takes the dative.

sentences.t: nun wollte sie so lange suchen und über Berg und Thal wandern, bis sie ihn fände.
sentences.l: now she would search so long and wander over hill and dale until she found him.
sentences.i: now she meant to search on and wander over hill and dale until she found him.
sentences.n: über Berg und Thal is the set phrase, our “over hill and dale”; Thal is the 1857 spelling of Tal. fände is the subjunctive of finden, the mood of what is still to come.

sentences.t: Da sprach die alte Dicke
sentences.l: Then the old fat one said
sentences.n: die alte Dicke — the same big toad as before, with alte added. The call that follows is the same verse again, changed only in its last line.

sentences.t:
„Jungfer grün und klein,
Hutzelbein,
Hutzelbeins Hündchen,
hutzel hin und her,
bring mir die große Schachtel her.“
sentences.l:
“Maiden green and small,
Shrivel-leg,
Shrivel-leg’s little dog,
shrivel here and there,
bring me the big box here.”
sentences.i:
“Maiden green and small,
Shrivel-leg,
Shrivel-leg’s little dog,
hop here and there,
bring me the great box here.”
sentences.n: As before, but the last line is now bring mir die große Schachtel her in place of laß geschwind sehen wer draußen wär — the charm is a summons, and what is summoned changes with the need. It still rhymes her with her, this time on the same word. herbringen is split: bring … her.

sentences.t: Da gieng die kleine hin und brachte die Schachtel herbeigetragen.
sentences.l: Then the little one went there and brought the box carried along.
sentences.i: Then the little one went and fetched the box, carrying it in.
sentences.n: die kleine, an adjective used as a name again: the little one. brachte … herbeigetragen doubles the verbs — “brought carried here” — where English needs one verb and a participle.

sentences.t: Hernach gaben sie ihr Essen und Trinken, und brachten sie zu einem schönen gemachten Bett, das war wie Seide und Sammet, da legte sie sich hinein und schlief in Gottes Namen.
sentences.l: Afterward they gave her food and drink, and brought her to a beautifully made bed, that was like silk and velvet, there she laid herself in it and slept in God’s name.
sentences.i: Afterwards they gave her food and drink and brought her to a beautifully made bed that was like silk and velvet; she laid herself down in it and slept in God’s name.
sentences.n: Essen und Trinken are infinitives used as nouns, “eating and drinking”, so food and drink. Sammet is the older form of Samt, velvet. in Gottes Namen schlafen: she sleeps commending herself to God, the ordinary pious phrase and not a flourish.

sentences.t: Als der Tag kam, stieg sie auf, und gab ihr die alte Itsche drei Nadeln aus der großen Schachtel, die sollte sie mitnehmen;
sentences.l: When the day came, she rose up, and the old toad gave her three needles out of the big box, those she should take along;
sentences.i: When day came she rose, and the old toad gave her three needles out of the great box, which she was to take with her;
sentences.n: aufsteigen — to rise, to get up (separable: stieg … auf). die sollte sie mitnehmen leads with the demonstrative die, “those”; German can begin with the object this way, English has to say “which”. The sentence runs on.

sentences.t: sie würden ihr nöthig thun, denn sie müßte über einen hohen gläsernen Berg und über drei schneidende Schwerter und über ein großes Wasser:
sentences.l: they would do her need, for she would have to over a high glassy mountain and over three cutting swords and over a great water:
sentences.i: she would have need of them, for she would have to cross a high mountain of glass and three cutting swords and a great water:
sentences.n: nöthig thun is an old turn — “to do need”, that is, to be needed, to come in useful; nöthig is the 1857 spelling of nötig. After müßte the verb of motion is left out again, and the literal line leaves the gap open rather than filling it.

sentences.t: wenn sie das durchsetzte, würde sie ihren Liebsten wiederkriegen.
sentences.l: if she carried that through, she would get her dearest back again.
sentences.i: if she carried that through, she would win her beloved back.
sentences.n: durchsetzen — to carry a thing through, to see it out (separable). wiederkriegen, to get back, is homely where Liebsten is high; the tales mix the two registers without a qualm.

sentences.t: Nun gab sie hiermit drei Theile (Stücke), die sollte sie recht in Acht nehmen, nämlich drei große Nadeln, ein Pflugrad und drei Nüsse.
sentences.l: Now with this she gave [her] three parts (pieces), those she should take right good care of, namely three big needles, a plough-wheel and three nuts.
sentences.i: Now with that she gave her three items, which she was to take good care of — namely three great needles, a plough-wheel and three nuts.
sentences.n: The parenthesis (Stücke) is the Grimms’ own: they gloss their own Theile, “parts”, with the plainer Stücke, “pieces”, for their readers — round brackets are theirs, square brackets in these translations are supplied here, and the bracketed [her] marks a dative the German simply leaves out. in Acht nehmen — to take care of, to look after. Das Pflugrad is the wheel of a wheeled plough, and it will be ridden like a wheel.

sentences.t: Hiermit reiste sie ab, und wie sie vor den gläsernen Berg kam, der so glatt war, steckte sie die drei Nadeln als hinter die Füße und dann wieder vorwärts, und gelangte so hinüber,
sentences.l: With this she travelled off, and when she came before the glassy mountain, which was so smooth, she stuck the three needles each time behind her feet and then forward again, and so got across,
sentences.i: With that she set off, and when she came to the mountain of glass, which was so smooth, she set the three needles behind her feet and then in front again, and so got across,
sentences.n: abreisen — to set off on a journey (separable: reiste … ab). The little word als in steckte sie die drei Nadeln als hinter die Füße is not the ordinary als: in Hessian speech, which is where the Grimms heard these tales, als does duty for immer, “each time, over and over”, and that suits the sequence als … und dann wieder. The reading is not certain, but the picture is plain even where the word is not: the needles are planted for footholds, then pulled up and set ahead of her, again and again.

sentences.t: und als sie hinüber war, steckte sie sie an einen Ort, den sie wohl in Acht nahm.
sentences.l: and when she was across, she stuck them in a place that she took good note of.
sentences.i: and when she was across, she put them in a place she marked well.
sentences.n: steckte sie sie — the first sie is the girl, the second the needles, standing side by side with nothing to tell them apart but the sense. in Acht nehmen here is to take note of, to keep in mind; she will want the needles again on the way back.

sentences.t: Danach kam sie vor die drei schneidenden Schwerter, da stellte sie sich auf ihr Pflugrad und rollte hinüber.
sentences.l: After that she came before the three cutting swords, then she placed herself on her plough-wheel and rolled across.
sentences.i: After that she came to the three cutting swords; she set herself on her plough-wheel and rolled across.
sentences.n: sich stellen — to place oneself, to take one’s stand. schneidend is the present participle of schneiden, “cutting”: the swords stand edge upward, and the wheel carries her over them.

sentences.t: Endlich kam sie vor ein großes Wasser, und wie sie übergefahren war, in ein großes schönes Schloß.
sentences.l: At last she came before a great water, and when she had been ferried across, into a great beautiful castle.
sentences.i: At last she came to a great water, and when she had been ferried across, [she came] into a great and beautiful castle.
sentences.n: The verb of the last clause is left out, and kam from the opening has to carry over; the bracketed [she came] is supplied here so that the English can stand, and is not in the 1857 text. übergefahren, from überfahren, is to be ferried over.

sentences.t: Sie gieng hinein und hielt um einen Dienst an, sie wär eine arme Magd und wollte sich gerne vermiethen; sie wußte aber daß der Königssohn drinne war, den sie erlöst hatte aus dem eisernen Ofen im großen Wald.
sentences.l: She went in and applied for a place, [saying] she was a poor maid and would gladly hire herself out; but she knew that the king’s son was inside, whom she had delivered out of the iron stove in the great forest.
sentences.i: She went in and asked for a place, saying she was a poor maid and would gladly hire herself out; but she knew that the king’s son was in there, the one she had freed from the iron stove in the great forest.
sentences.n: um einen Dienst anhalten — to apply for a position (separable: hielt … an). The reported speech starts with no “saying” at all, marked only by the subjunctive wär; the bracketed [saying] is supplied here. sich vermiethen (1857 for vermieten) is to hire oneself out as a servant. drinne is a spoken form of drinnen, inside.

sentences.t: Also ward sie angenommen zum Küchenmädchen für geringen Lohn.
sentences.l: So she was taken on as kitchen-maid for low wages.
sentences.n: annehmen — to take on, to engage (past participle angenommen). zum Küchenmädchen — “as kitchen-maid”, with zu where English says “as”. The king’s daughter is now a servant in her own bridegroom’s house, and the tale says nothing about it.

sentences.t: Nun hatte der Königssohn schon wieder eine andere an der Seite, die wollte er heirathen, denn er dachte sie wäre längst gestorben.
sentences.l: Now the king’s son already had another one at his side again, that one he wanted to marry, for he thought she had long since died.
sentences.i: By now the king’s son had another at his side already, whom he meant to marry, for he thought she had long since died.
sentences.n: an der Seite haben — to have at one’s side, that is, to have taken up with. die wollte er heirathen leads with the demonstrative die, “that one”. wäre gestorben is subjunctive: what he thought, not what was so.

sentences.t: Abends, wie sie aufgewaschen hatte und fertig war, fühlte sie in die Tasche und fand die drei Nüsse, welche ihr die alte Itsche gegeben hatte.
sentences.l: In the evening, when she had washed up and was finished, she felt into her pocket and found the three nuts which the old toad had given her.
sentences.i: In the evening, when she had washed up and was done, she felt in her pocket and found the three nuts the old toad had given her.
sentences.n: aufwaschen — to wash up the dishes (separable). in die Tasche fühlen takes the accusative because the hand moves into the pocket: German marks the motion by the case.

sentences.t: Biß eine auf und wollte den Kern essen, siehe, da war ein stolzes königliches Kleid drin.
sentences.l: [She] bit one open and wanted to eat the kernel — see, there was a splendid royal gown in it.
sentences.i: She cracked one open and was about to eat the kernel — and behold, there was a splendid royal gown inside.
sentences.n: The subject is left out at the head again — Biß eine auf, with no sie; the bracketed [She] is supplied here. aufbeißen is to bite open (separable: biß … auf). siehe is the old imperative of sehen, the teller pointing: behold. stolz of a thing is “splendid, stately”, not the pride of a person.

sentences.t: Wies nun die Braut hörte, kam sie und hielt um das Kleid an und wollte es kaufen und sagte, „es wäre kein Kleid für eine Dienstmagd.“
sentences.l: When the bride now heard it, she came and applied for the gown and wanted to buy it and said, “it was no gown for a serving-maid.”
sentences.i: When the bride heard of it she came and asked for the gown and wanted to buy it, and said it was no gown for a serving-maid.
sentences.n: Wies is wie es, “when … it”. anhalten um again, this time for the gown and not a place. wäre is subjunctive, the bride’s words as reported, although the printed quotation marks put them straight into her mouth.

sentences.t: Da sprach sie nein sie wollts nicht verkaufen, doch wann sie ihr einerlei (ein Ding) wollte erlauben, so sollte sies haben, nämlich eine Nacht in der Kammer ihres Bräutigams zu schlafen.
sentences.l: Then she said no, she would not sell it, yet if she would allow her one thing (a thing), then she should have it, namely to sleep one night in the chamber of her bridegroom.
sentences.i: Then she said no, she would not sell it; but if the bride would allow her one thing, she should have it — namely to sleep one night in her bridegroom’s chamber.
sentences.n: The parenthesis (ein Ding) is the Grimms’ own again, glossing einerlei — here used as a noun, “one thing, a single thing” — with a plainer word. wann stands in the older sense of wenn, “if”. wollts is wollte es and sies is sie es.

sentences.t: Die Braut erlaubt es ihr, weil das Kleid so schön war und sie noch keins so hatte.
sentences.l: The bride allows it to her, because the gown was so beautiful and she had none yet like it.
sentences.i: The bride allowed it, because the gown was so beautiful and she had none like it.
sentences.n: erlaubt is present tense in the middle of a past narrative — the teller slips into the present for a moment, which German does easily and which the literal line keeps. keins so — “none such”, none like it.

sentences.t: Wies nun Abend war, sagte sie zu ihrem Bräutigam „das närrische Mädchen will in deiner Kammer schlafen.“
sentences.l: When it was now evening, she said to her bridegroom “the foolish girl wants to sleep in your chamber.”
sentences.i: When evening came she said to her bridegroom, “the foolish girl wants to sleep in your chamber.”
sentences.n: närrisch — foolish, cracked, from der Narr, the fool. deiner: the bride says du to the king’s son, as betrothed people do.

sentences.t: „Wenn du’s zufrieden bist, bin ichs auch“ sprach er.
sentences.l: “If you are content with it, I am too,” he said.
sentences.i: “If you are content with it, so am I,” he said.
sentences.n: etwas zufrieden sein is the older construction — to be content with a thing, with no preposition at all. du’s is du es and ichs is ich es; the apostrophe in du’s is the printed text’s own.

sentences.t: Sie gab aber dem Mann ein Glas Wein, in das sie einen Schlaftrunk gethan hatte.
sentences.l: But she gave the man a glass of wine, into which she had put a sleeping-draught.
sentences.n: gethan is the 1857 spelling of getan, from thun, modern tun. ein Glas Wein sets the measure and what is measured side by side with no “of”. dem Mann is her bridegroom.

sentences.t: Also giengen beide in die Kammer schlafen, und er schlief so fest, daß sie ihn nicht erwecken konnte.
sentences.l: So both went into the chamber to sleep, and he slept so fast that she could not wake him.
sentences.i: So the two of them went into the chamber to sleep, and he slept so soundly that she could not wake him.
sentences.n: schlafen stands as a bare infinitive of purpose after giengen — “went to sleep”, that is, went in order to sleep. fest schlafen is to sleep soundly.

sentences.t: Sie weinte die ganze Nacht und rief „ich habe dich erlöst aus dem wilden Wald und aus einem eisernen Ofen, ich habe dich gesucht und bin gegangen über einen gläsernen Berg, über drei schneidende Schwerter und über ein großes Wasser, ehe ich dich gefunden habe, und willst mich doch nicht hören.“
sentences.l: She wept the whole night and called “I have delivered you out of the wild forest and out of an iron stove, I have sought you and have gone over a glassy mountain, over three cutting swords and over a great water, before I found you, and yet will not hear me.”
sentences.i: She wept the whole night through and called, “I set you free from the wild forest and from an iron stove; I have searched for you and gone over a mountain of glass, over three cutting swords and over a great water before I found you — and still you will not hear me.”
sentences.n: und willst mich doch nicht hören drops the subject du where it is plain from the verb ending; doch is the little word of protest, “and yet”. bin gegangen forms its perfect with sein, as verbs of motion do. The whole journey is recited back in one breath, and it will be recited twice more.

sentences.t: Die Bedienten saßen vor der Stubenthüre und hörten wie sie so die ganze Nacht weinte und sagtens am Morgen ihrem Herrn.
sentences.l: The servants sat before the parlour door and heard how she wept so the whole night and said it in the morning to their master.
sentences.i: The servants sat outside the parlour door and heard how she wept like that the whole night through, and in the morning they told their master.
sentences.n: sagtens is sagten es, “said it”. die Stubenthüre, 1857 for Stubentür, is the door of the Stube, the living room, off which the sleeping chamber opens; the servants sit there through the night.

sentences.t: Und wie sie am andern Abend aufgewaschen hatte, biß sie die zweite Nuß auf, da war noch ein weit schöneres Kleid drin; wie das die Braut sah, wollte sie es auch kaufen.
sentences.l: And when she had washed up on the next evening, she bit open the second nut, and there was a far more beautiful gown in it; when the bride saw that, she wanted to buy it too.
sentences.i: And when she had washed up the next evening she cracked open the second nut, and there was a far more beautiful gown inside; when the bride saw it, she wanted to buy that one too.
sentences.n: am andern Abend — “on the other evening”, that is, the next; ander in the tales often means the next in a series. weit before a comparative is “far”, as in English.

sentences.t: Aber Geld wollte das Mädchen nicht und bat sich aus daß es noch einmal in der Kammer des Bräutigams schlafen dürfte.
sentences.l: But money the girl did not want, and asked out for herself that it might sleep once more in the bridegroom’s chamber.
sentences.i: But the girl would take no money, and begged leave to sleep once more in the bridegroom’s chamber.
sentences.n: Geld stands first as the object, which German allows for emphasis. das Mädchen is grammatically neuter, so the pronoun that follows is es, “it”, of a girl; the literal line keeps the German’s “it” and the idiomatic line says “she”, as English must.

sentences.t: Die Braut gab ihm aber einen Schlaftrunk, und er schlief so fest, daß er nichts hören konnte.
sentences.l: But the bride gave him a sleeping-draught, and he slept so fast that he could hear nothing.
sentences.i: But the bride gave him a sleeping-draught again, and he slept so soundly that he could hear nothing.
sentences.n: The second night is told in the same words as the first, only shorter — the tale repeats and pares as it goes.

sentences.t: Das Küchenmädchen weinte aber die ganze Nacht, und rief „ich habe dich erlöst aus einem Walde und aus einem eisernen Ofen, ich habe dich gesucht und bin gegangen über einen gläsernen Berg, über drei schneidende Schwerter und über ein großes Wasser, ehe ich dich gefunden habe, und du willst mich doch nicht hören.“
sentences.l: But the kitchen-maid wept the whole night, and called “I have delivered you out of a forest and out of an iron stove, I have sought you and have gone over a glassy mountain, over three cutting swords and over a great water, before I found you, and you will not hear me.”
sentences.i: But the kitchen-maid wept the whole night through and called, “I set you free from a forest and from an iron stove; I have searched for you and gone over a mountain of glass, over three cutting swords and over a great water before I found you — and you will not hear me.”
sentences.n: The lament comes again almost word for word: dem wilden Wald has become einem Walde, and this time the du is spoken, du willst mich doch nicht hören, where the first time it was left out. Small shifts like these are how the tales mark a second telling.

sentences.t: Die Bedienten saßen vor der Stubenthüre und hörten wie sie so die ganze Nacht weinte, und sagtens am Morgen ihrem Herrn.
sentences.l: The servants sat before the parlour door and heard how she wept so the whole night, and said it in the morning to their master.
sentences.i: The servants sat outside the parlour door and heard how she wept like that the whole night through, and in the morning they told their master.
sentences.n: The line is repeated exactly as before, with only a comma added in the printed text — and what the printed text has is what stands here.

sentences.t: Und als sie am dritten Abend aufgewaschen hatte, biß sie die dritte Nuß auf, da war ein noch schöneres Kleid drin, das starrte von purem Gold.
sentences.l: And when she had washed up on the third evening, she bit open the third nut, and there was a still more beautiful gown in it, it was stiff with pure gold.
sentences.i: And when she had washed up on the third evening she cracked open the third nut, and there was a still more beautiful gown inside, stiff with pure gold.
sentences.n: starren von — to be stiff with, to bristle with; of cloth so heavily worked with gold that it would stand up by itself. purem is the dative of pur, pure — plain High German here, with no dialect about it. drin is the contracted darin, “in it”.

sentences.t: Wie die Braut das sah, wollte sie es haben, das Mädchen aber gab es nur hin, wenn es zum drittenmal dürfte in der Kammer des Bräutigams schlafen.
sentences.l: When the bride saw that, she wanted to have it, but the girl only gave it away if it might sleep for the third time in the bridegroom’s chamber.
sentences.i: When the bride saw it she wanted to have it, but the girl would only give it up if she might sleep a third time in the bridegroom’s chamber.
sentences.n: hingeben — to give away, to hand over (separable: gab … hin). Again es for das Mädchen: the neuter pronoun follows the grammar of the word, not the sex of the girl.

sentences.t: Der Königssohn aber hütete sich und ließ den Schlaftrunk vorbei laufen.
sentences.l: But the king’s son was on his guard and let the sleeping-draught run past.
sentences.i: But the king’s son was on his guard and let the sleeping-draught go by untouched.
sentences.n: sich hüten — to be on one’s guard, to take care. etwas vorbei laufen lassen — to let a thing run past; here to let the drink go by without drinking it. Nothing is said of how he came to be warned, though the servants have told him twice.

sentences.t: Wie sie nun anfieng zu weinen und zu rufen „liebster Schatz, ich habe dich erlöst aus dem grausamen wilden Walde und aus einem eisernen Ofen,“ so sprang der Königssohn auf und sprach „du bist die rechte, du bist mein, und ich bin dein.“
sentences.l: When she now began to weep and to call “dearest treasure, I have delivered you out of the cruel wild forest and out of an iron stove,” then the king’s son sprang up and said “you are the right one, you are mine, and I am yours.”
sentences.i: When she began to weep and to call, “dearest heart, I set you free from the cruel wild forest and from an iron stove,” the king’s son sprang up and said, “you are the right one; you are mine and I am yours.”
sentences.n: Schatz, “treasure”, is the ordinary German endearment for a sweetheart. aufspringen — to spring up (separable: sprang … auf). du bist mein und ich bin dein comes back from the moment of his release, and the ring is closed.

sentences.t: Darauf setzte er sich noch in der Nacht mit ihr in einen Wagen, und der falschen Braut nahmen sie die Kleider weg, daß sie nicht aufstehen konnte.
sentences.l: Thereupon he set himself with her in a carriage that same night, and from the false bride they took the clothes away, so that she could not get up.
sentences.i: Thereupon he got into a carriage with her that very night, and they took the false bride’s clothes away, so that she could not get up.
sentences.n: der falschen Braut is the dative of the one deprived: German takes the clothes “from her”, where English makes it a possessive. wegnehmen is split, nahmen … weg. The measure is practical rather than cruel — without her clothes she cannot follow them.

sentences.t: Als sie zu dem großen Wasser kamen, da schifften sie hinüber, und vor den drei schneidenden Schwertern, da setzten sie sich aufs Pflugrad, und vor dem gläsernen Berg, da steckten sie die drei Nadeln hinein.
sentences.l: When they came to the great water, then they shipped across, and before the three cutting swords, then they set themselves on the plough-wheel, and before the glassy mountain, then they stuck the three needles in.
sentences.i: When they came to the great water they ferried across; and at the three cutting swords they set themselves on the plough-wheel; and at the mountain of glass they stuck the three needles in.
sentences.n: schiffen — to go by ship, to ferry over. The three obstacles are met in the same shape three times, da … da … da, and in the reverse order from her outward journey; the needles she took such care to mark the place of are used again.

sentences.t: So gelangten sie endlich zu dem alten kleinen Häuschen, aber wie sie hineintraten, wars ein großes Schloß: die Itschen waren alle erlöst und lauter Königskinder und waren in voller Freude.
sentences.l: So they came at last to the old little house, but when they stepped inside, it was a great castle: the toads were all delivered and nothing but king’s children and were in full joy.
sentences.i: So at last they came to the old cottage; but when they stepped inside, it was a great castle: the toads were all released from their spell and were king’s children, every one, and in full joy.
sentences.n: hineintreten — to step inside (separable: traten hinein). wars is war es. lauter means “nothing but, all of them”: the toads were king’s children to the last one, and were under a spell just as the king’s son was.

sentences.t: Da ward Vermählung gehalten, und sie blieben in dem Schloß, das war viel größer als ihres Vaters Schloß.
sentences.l: Then the wedding was held, and they stayed in the castle, that was much bigger than her father’s castle.
sentences.i: Then the wedding was held, and they stayed in the castle, which was much bigger than her father’s castle.
sentences.n: ward … gehalten is the passive with the older ward; Vermählung halten is the set phrase for holding a wedding. das war: the demonstrative das opens the clause where English uses “which”.

sentences.t: Weil aber der Alte jammerte daß er allein bleiben sollte, so fuhren sie weg und holten ihn zu sich, und hatten zwei Königreiche und lebten in gutem Ehestand.
sentences.l: But because the old man lamented that he should stay alone, they drove away and fetched him to themselves, and had two kingdoms and lived in good wedlock.
sentences.i: But because the old man lamented that he was to be left alone, they drove off and fetched him to live with them; and they had two kingdoms and lived in good wedlock.
sentences.n: der Alte — the adjective as a noun again, “the old man”, her father. zu sich holen — to fetch someone to oneself, to take them in. der Ehestand is the married state, wedlock: the tale ends on the settled word rather than on happiness.

sentences.t:
Da kam eine Maus,
Das Märchen war aus.
sentences.l:
Then came a mouse,
The tale was out.
sentences.i:
Then along came a mouse,
and the tale was done.
sentences.n: A closing rhyme-tag of the kind tellers use to break the spell and hand the room back; Maus rhymes with aus, which the English cannot do and does not try. aus sein is “to be over, at an end”. The two lines are printed as verse and stand as verse here.

glossary.allein: allein — alone; at the head of a clause, the older ‘only, but’ (allein der war nicht zu finden)
glossary.aus: aus — out of, from; aus sein — to be over, at an end (das Märchen war aus)
glossary.braten: der Braten — the roast, roast meat (noun; braten: to roast)
glossary.bring: bringen — bring (imperative sg.; here herbringen, to bring here: bring … her)
glossary.drin: drin — in it, inside (contraction of darin)
glossary.einerlei: einerlei — one thing, a single thing (here a noun, glossed by the Grimms themselves as ‘ein Ding’; ordinarily: all the same)
glossary.essen: essen — to eat; das Essen — food, eating (Essen und Trinken: food and drink)
glossary.fest: fest — firm, fast, tight (adj./adv.; fest schlafen: to sleep soundly); das Fest — festival, feast
glossary.fort: fort — away, off, gone; onward, on (weiter fort: further on; fortschrappen: to scrape on)
glossary.fuhren: fahren — drove, travelled (3rd pl. past; here wegfahren, to drive off: fuhren … weg)
glossary.gedachte: gedenken — intended, had in mind (3rd sg. past, with an infinitive; also: to be mindful of)
glossary.gedeckt: decken — laid, set (past part.; einen Tisch decken: to lay a table; also: covered)
glossary.geringen: gering — small, slight, low (inflected; für geringen Lohn: for low wages)
glossary.geringste: gering — slight, small (superlative das geringste: the least little bit)
glossary.hielt: anhalten — applied for, asked for (3rd sg. past; separable: hielt … an, um etwas anhalten); halten alone: to hold, to stop
glossary.kasten: der Kasten — chest, box (dat. sg.; here the iron stove, named a second way)
glossary.kehren: kehren — to turn (here zurück kehren = zurückkehren, to return)
glossary.leben: leben — to live, to live on (nichts mehr zu leben: nothing left to live on); das Leben: life
glossary.purem: pur — pure (dat. sg.; von purem Gold: of pure gold)
glossary.riefs: rufen — rief es, it called (3rd sg. past + the clitic es glued onto the verb)
glossary.s: s — ’s, a clipped es or das written onto the word before it (du’s = du es)
glossary.schöner: schön — more beautiful (comparative schöner; noch schöner als: even more beautiful than)
glossary.stolzes: stolz — proud; of a thing, splendid, stately (adj., neut. inflected; ein stolzes Kleid)
glossary.trinken: trinken — to drink; das Trinken — drink (the infinitive used as a noun)
glossary.voller: voll — full (adj.; inflected here, in voller Freude: in full joy; also indeclinable voller + noun: full of)
glossary.ward: werden — was, became (3rd sg. past, archaic for wurde; with a past participle it makes the passive: ward verwünscht, was cursed)
glossary.weg: weg — away, off (adv. and separable prefix: wegnehmen); der Weg — way, path (auf dem Weg: on the way)
